name: journal-thirteen-letters-or-fourteen.json
content:
Most Protestant Bibles give Paul thirteen letters and print Hebrews beside them with no author named. For centuries the church counted fourteen. Davidson's lists show how the number rose and how it fell.

Ten, then thirteen

Marcion brought ten letters to Rome in 144, and Hebrews was not among them.1 Davidson puts the Muratorian canon at about 170. It names thirteen letters of Paul, and "The epistle to the Hebrews, 1 and 2 Peter, 1 John and James are not named."2

On Hebrews he says plainly: "The Epistle to the Hebrews was rejected in the west."3 He thinks the letter "to the Alexandrians" that the Muratorian list rejects is "probably the epistle to the Hebrews".4

The East, and Augustine

The East was more willing. Of Augustine, Davidson says he specified "the Pauline epistles as fourteen, and so reckoning that to the Hebrews as the apostle's". Augustine knew that some were uncertain, and he was "influenced to admit it as canonical by the authority of the Oriental churches."5

That is a candid reason. Augustine took Hebrews because the Eastern churches did, and the Western doubt gave way to their custom.

Fourteen, fixed

The African synods then wrote it down. Davidson reports that the council at Carthage in 419 "repeated the former list of books with a single alteration, viz., fourteen epistles of Paul (instead of thirteen)."6 The Damasus form of the list has fourteen. The Gelasian form lacks Hebrews.7

Even the place of the letter moved. Davidson prints several orders. In Augustine and the Vulgate Hebrews follows Philemon, and in other lists it stands before the pastoral letters.8

Fourteen, doubted

The Reformers took the number apart again. Davidson says Luther "thought the epistle to the Hebrews was neither Paul's nor an apostle's, but proceeded from an excellent and learned man who may have been the disciple of apostles."9 Calvin did not think Paul wrote it, yet held it canonical.10

Scholars today generally treat the author of Hebrews as unknown.11 A missionary who counts fourteen letters of Paul is repeating the church's long custom. Its own early lists, east and west, did not agree on the number.

Verdict. The count of Paul's letters was ten for Marcion, thirteen for the Muratorian list and fourteen for Augustine and Carthage. Fourteen is a decision of the fourth and fifth centuries, and Hebrews never names its author.
